#7503. 11th Circuit tosses ex-Georgia Tech professor’s lawsuit against university auditors

The 11th Circuit panel found that the former Georgia Tech professor's racketeering charges stemmed from an independent investigation by state authorities, not a university audit.

(CN) â An 11th Circuit panel rejected a former Georgia Tech professorâs suit against two university auditors he blamed for his arrest in a racketeering case.

Chief U.S. Circuit Judge William Pryor wrote in a unanimous opinion issued Monday that Joy Laskar failed to establish that the auditors, Phillip Hurd and Patrick Jenkins, conducted the investigation that led to his prosecution. Laskarâs charges stemmed from an independent investigation conducted by state authorities â not the university officials’ internal audit or their report of suspected misconduct, the panel found.

âBefore obtaining an arrest warrant, Agent Vorrasi and McLaughlin conducted an independent investigation,â the George W. Bush appointee wrote in the opinion. âThey reviewed the same documents reviewed during the audit. They spent four months analyzing thousands of documents, deposing Sayana employees and consulting other university officials.â

Laskar was director of the Georgia Electronic Design Center, a research center where tech companies collaborate with researchers after paying membership dues. He was also co-founder and president of Sayana, a company that designed and developed high-frequency microchips.

In 2009, Georgia Tech began investigating a $600,000 shortfall at the center, according to court filings. Hurd and Jenkins learned during their audit that Sayana had billed the design center more than $1 million for the manufacture of prototype microchips which were later sent to a South Korean institute, which paid for the prototypes and research.

Laskar failed to disclose in conflict-of-interest reports filed with the university between 2007 and 2010 that he had a 42.5% stake in Sayana, according to the auditors. Sayana also did not pay membership fees to use the centerâs resources.

The auditors reported the suspected malfeasance to the university, which in turn sent the report to the Georgia Department of Law.

Laskar was charged in 2010 with two counts of racketeering, but a Superior Court judge dismissed the case four years later after finding the statute of limitations barred the charges.

Laskar filed a civil rights action against the auditors in 2018 in the Northern District of Georgia, claiming the government employees intentionally provided false and misleading information to law enforcement.

U.S. District Judge William M. Ray, a Donald Trump appointee, initially dismissed the case because Laskar did not receive a âfavorable terminationâ in criminal court, or a finding of innocence, which could maintain a malicious prosecution suit. The decision was reversed on appeal, but Ray dismissed it again last year after finding Laskar failed to support his claims that the auditors operated as law enforcement officers.

The 11th Circuit panel appeared skeptical of Laskarâs arguments during a hearing this month.

U.S. Circuit Judge Embry Kidd, a Joe Biden appointee, suggested the auditorsâ recommendation was no different from any other tip to law enforcement.

âSometimes investigations rely heavily on information provided by others,â he said. âThat does not mean that the decision by the investigator wasnât independent of the people providing the information.â

Pryor said it did not matter if the auditors provided advice and information to state authorities. The investigators specifically stated that their warrant application was based on their independent investigation and their own assessment of the evidence.

Pryor filed a separate concurring opinion Monday addressing the U.S. Supreme Courtâs decision in Thompson v. Clark, which determined a plaintiff only needs to show that a prosecution ended without a conviction to establish the “favorable termination” element for a malicious prosecution case.

Pryor defended the use of the common-law tort of malicious prosecution as the appropriate analogy for constitutional claims involving seizures pursuant to legal process, such as arrests based on warrants.

He distinguished those claims from challenges to warrantless arrests, explaining that the two types of seizures involve different legal considerations.

U.S. Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa, a Trump appointee, rounded out the panel.

#7500. Federal judge says he can’t stop Trump’s ICC judge sanctions

President Donald Trump imposed the sanctions on judges after the ICC pursued investigations involving U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and Israeli leaders over the war in Gaza.

MANHATTAN (CN) âÂ A federal judge in New York on Monday said he doesn’t have the power to stop President Donald Trump from imposing sanctions on judges of the International Criminal Court in the form of frozen bank accounts, canceled credit cards and blocked travel.

Trump declared a national emergency in a 2025 executive order with respect to any ICC effort to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute “any United States person” unless the U.S. formally consents or becomes a state party to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC in 2002 to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Judges Kimberly Prost, Solomy Bossa and Reine Alapini-Gansou of the ICC turned to the U.S. courts asking to be removed from the sanctions list, unblock their frozen property and bar Trump from enforcing measures against them. But U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman dismissed all but one of their claims and denied a preliminary injunction, finding “deference here is owed not only to the president but also to Congress.”

“In short, whatever the courtâs own assessment of the circumstances may be, plaintiffsâ allegations do not permit the court to hold that the president acted ultra vires when he declared a national emergency to address what he determined to be an ‘unusual and extraordinary threat, which has its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States,’ to the national security, foreign policy, or economy of the United States,” Furman wrote in a 37-page order.

Each judge was sanctioned over a different decision. Prost, of Canada, and Bossa, of the Republic of Uganda, joined a 2020 appeals ruling that allowed the ICC prosecutor to investigate suspected war crimes and crimes against humanity in Afghanistan. Alapini-Gansou, of the Republic of Benin, sat on the panel that approved arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.

The trio of judges sued under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, U.S. Constitution and Administrative Procedure Act. Furman, a Barack Obama appointee, dismissed the due process and takings clause claims, but preserved the plaintiffs’ APA claim accusing the federal government of arbitrary and capricious sanctions designations. That count is premature, the judge said, since it must be decided on the full administrative record that was before Secretary of State Marco Rubio when he made the decision.

Furman noted there are three other cases in Manhattan federal court involving challenges to Trump’s executive order, but unlike the others, the trio of judges don’t bring First Amendment claims and are challenging the order in its entirety.

Those other, earlier lawsuits filed by U.S. human rights advocates resulted in rulings barring the administration from enforcing the order against Americans providing speech-based services to the ICC.

Trump signed Executive Order 14203 on Feb. 6, 2025, after the ICC pursued investigations involving U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and Israeli leaders over the war in Gaza.

After first sanctioning ICC prosecutor Karim Khan, the White House expanded its list to include the international courtâs two deputy prosecutors, eight judges, U.N. Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and three Palestinian human rights organizations: Al-Haq, Al Mezan Center for Human Rights and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights.

The sanctions formally freeze U.S.-based assets and bar Americans from providing funds or services. The judges say their effects ripple across global banks, payment systems and technology companies that rely heavily on the U.S. financial system.

âThe sanctions regime punishes Judges Prost, Bossa and Alapini-Gansou for having done nothing more than â when called upon to adjudicate matters before them â faithfully discharge their judicial offices by rendering decisions with which the administration disagrees,â the judges say in their lawsuit.

In addition to arguing that the sanctions strike at the independence of international courts by punishing judges for carrying out their duties, the judges say Trump’s order disrupts ICC investigations that Republican and Democratic administrations alike have backed over the years, including cases involving Sudan, Libya, Uganda, Mali, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Ukraine.

OAKLAND, Calif. (CN) â In a final hour Hail Mary in a nearly two-monthlong bribery trial featuring ex-Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao, the defense tried to call the credibility of the prosecution’s star witness into question.

But Chief U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers didn’t seem particularly convinced on Monday by a motion to dismiss the case based on what the defense called Mario Juarez’s false testimony.

Juarez, a longtime East Bay political player, claims he entered into a bribery scheme with father and son David and Andy Duong to secure city contracts for their shipping container homes company.

The Duongs, along with Thao and her romantic partner Andre Jones, charged with crimes including conspiracy, bribery, fraud and making a false statement to a government official.

All four co-defendants have pleaded not guilty. Thao faces a maximum sentence of 95 years in prison if convicted on all charges. Thao, Jones and the Duongs waived the right to testify in their own defense.

âHeâs a con artist, you did a very good job,â Rogers said referring to the defenseâs attack of Juarezâs credibility. âItâs not clear that the government is going to a get a conviction, or a verdict, period. This jury could hang.â

Juarez, who became an FBI informant reportedly after a falling out with the Duongs, testified he and the Duongs bribed Thao in exchange for lucrative contracts with the city to buy up to 300 container units and an extension of the Duongs’ waste management company, California Waste Solutions. Jonesâ supposed role included collecting the bribes for Thao through a âno-showâ job at the container home company, Evolutionary Homes.

Now in the seventh week of trial, David Duongâs attorney Jeffrey Schenk also questioned IRS Special Agent Christine Stegner about a spreadsheet she created to reconcile Juarezâs Evolutionary Homes expense reports to the Duongs, which included doctored bank records.

The defense had previously asked to suppress Stegner’s previous testimony for the prosecution about how she formulated the spreadsheet in connection to her interviews with Juarez and hearing his testimony in court. Before the 15-person jury was seated Monday, Rogers denied the request to suppress.

Stegner also testified she didnât ask Juarez about the doctored bank records, nor was she asked to do so by the prosecution.

The defenseâs second witness, Luis Mejia Solis, a parking lot owner in East Oakland, testified through a Spanish court interpreter that he knew Juarez because he stored two box trucks in his lot.

Mejia testified he accompanied Juarez in a black BMW in May 2024 to an Oakland Embarcadero building, the headquarters of California Waste Solutions and Evolutionary Homes. He said Juarez tried to use a set of keys to get into the building, but they didnât work.

Mejia said during the incident Juarez got into an argument with âan Asian man,â but then abruptly ran back to the car and hid âa black metal objectâ he pulled from the back of his waistband and placed under the driverâs seat, saying he needed to âhide the gun.â

Juarez testified earlier in the trial during the incident that Duong associates showed up after Mejia left and beat him up, taking his watch and gold chain after he was locked out of the Evolutionary Homes office.

Juarez had also testified that part of the scheme was his funding of $75,000 for negative mailers about Thaoâs mayoral opponents, in exchange for Thaoâs promise to help Evolutionary Homes.

Former Thao staffer Brandon Harami testified Jones was a volunteer during Thaoâs mayoral campaign and helped produce mailers for the campaign that were different from Juarezâs negative mailers.

âI thought it was very poorly done,â Harami told Jonesâ attorney Mark Goldrosen.

âYou know better than to edit peopleâs features, especially a Black manâs features,â he said, referencing a mailer against Thao’s opponent Loren Taylor.

During Hamari’s cross-examination, Assistant U.S. Attorney Abraham Fine pointed out that Harami wasn’t present when two photographs at separate events were taken of Thao in conversation with Juarez and Andy Duong.

#7495. Quebec politicians decry court-ordered oath of allegiance to King Charles III

Quebec politicians will have to pledge an oath to King Charles III or risk legal battles over their laws.

MONTREAL (CN) â The Superior Court of Quebec ruled Monday that a 2022 law allowing members of the province’s National Assembly to pledge allegiance only to Quebecers, and not to the British king, is unconstitutional.

The decision sparked waves of protests from Quebec politicians, putting the upcoming legislative session in limbo.

Superior Court Justice Ian Demers found the provincial government overstepped its powers by abolishing the king’s oath without the approval of Ottawa and the other provinces. He ruled in favor of Lawrence David, a University of Ottawa law professor who challenged the legislation in August.

The judge agreed with David that suspending the law is necessary to avoid chaos in the National Assembly. The professor and founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute argued that laws adopted by members of the National Assembly who had not pledged their allegiance to King Charles III would be invalid and that the law violated Quebecers’ right to proper representation.

David also claimed the oath could be abolished only with the unanimous consent of the provinces and the federal Parliament, because the change encroached on the role of the lieutenant governor. Canada is a constitutional monarchy, and lieutenant governors represent the Crown.

The Legislature adopted Bill 4 in December 2022, after the three Parti QuÃ©bÃ©cois members elected that year refused to swear the oath required by the Constitution Act of 1867, and were barred from taking their seats in the National Assembly.

Quebec politicians appear to agree with the law. None of the 127 members of the National Assembly elected in October has sworn allegiance to the king. The court nonetheless found the law unconstitutional.

“The Constitution is not an Ã  la carte menu in which a subject complies with what suits them,” Demers wrote in his ruling. “Any other proposal would lead to constitutional disorder, or even chaos.”

“If the stay were not ordered, all laws passed by the National Assembly would be unconstitutional and would have to be reenacted,” he added, predicting the process would only “paralyze” the government and harm Quebecers.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, Parti Quebecois leader â and former lawyer â denounced the decision.

“The government of Quebec strongly condemns a ruling that clearly goes against the democratic will of Quebecers, who have expressed their desire to put an end to the disloyal act of swearing an oath to the British monarch and to the straitjacket of the monarchy in general,” the premier said in a statement released on social media in French.

In a press conference in Montreal on Monday, St-Pierre Plamondon called the ruling a “disgrace” and said he “cannot take an oath to the king of England.” He vowed to take all necessary measures to oppose the judgment.

The premier noted Quebec never signed the 1982 Canadian Constitution, and that the Constitutional Act of 1867 was imposed on the French-Canadian people after the British conquest of the French territory. He insists Quebecers should be allowed to follow the democratic process rather than be forced to follow rules imposed on them.

The legislative assembly set for Dec. 1 is now up in the air. Lawmakers must decide between swearing allegiance to the king and risking court challenges to every decision they make.

All the opposition parties also criticized the ruling and welcomed the government’s appeal, deploring that the decision could push back further the start of the National Assembly.

The Parti Quebecois has long been fighting the presence of the monarchy in Quebec. St-Pierre Plamondon promised earlier this year to abolish the Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec, or at least divert its resources to fight issues such as the homelessness crisis.

Courthouse News reporter Tatiana Mulowayi-Pelletier is based in Montreal, Canada.

#7493. Trump effort to toss hush-money conviction gets new life

The Second Circuit found that the late U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein erred when ruling it was too late for Trump to challenge his guilty verdict.

MANHATTAN (CN) â A federal appeals court on Monday gave President Donald Trump another shot at fighting his hush-money conviction, which infamously made him the first commander-in-chief in American history to be found guilty of criminal charges.

In a brief order, a Second Circuit panel found that U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, the now-deceased Bill Clinton appointee who rejected Trumpâs second attempt to remove the case from New York state court to federal court, was wrong to do so. Hellerstein had ruled that, since Trump had already been convicted and sentenced, the case was unavailable for federal removal.

âThe district court erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case after a federal officer defendant has been convicted,â the appellate panel ruled, adding that Hellerstein was also wrong in finding Trump lacked good cause to try removing the case again.

The case will now head back to the Southern District of New York, where a new federal judge will be assigned to make the call in Hellersteinâs place. Until then, the Second Circuit panel also ordered that Trumpâs state-level appellate efforts are paused âin order to preserve the status quo.â

U.S. Circuit Judges Raymond Lohier, a Barack Obama appointee, Jose Cabranes, a Bill Clinton appointee and John Walker, a George H.W. Bush appointee, were behind Mondayâs ruling.

The same panel heard oral arguments last week, in which Trumpâs attorney â Robert Giuffra of Sullivan & Cromwell â claimed that the case was destined for federal court since it dealt with the issue of presidential immunity.

âThe appeal of this unprecedented criminal case brought by the state of New York against the president of the United States belongs in federal court,â Giuffra said. âThis case involves important questions of presidential evidentiary immunity that arose out of the Supreme Courtâs landmark decision in Trump v. United States.â

Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg brought the state prosecution, which led to Trumpâs conviction in May 2024 on 34 counts of falsifying business records. According to prosecutors, Trump illegally disguised hush-money payments to porn star Stormy Daniels as routine legal expenses, part of his broader scheme to covertly influence the 2016 presidential election.

Trump claims this prosecution hinged on official acts he took as president, which runs afoul of the Supreme Courtâs 2024 ruling for broad presidential immunity.

Braggâs office declined to comment on Mondayâs ruling. Giuffra didnât immediately respond to requests for comment.

Trump could have faced prison time for the 34 felony convictions, but instead received a sentence of unconditional discharge after winning the 2024 presidency. Despite that, he has been steadfast in his efforts to overturn the criminal case, which Trump has called âthe most politically charged prosecution in our nationâs historyâ in legal briefs.

He first tried to remove the case to federal court pre-trial in 2023 â which Hellerstein denied.

Post-verdict, while his federal removal efforts persist, Trump is also trying his luck to get the verdict reversed the state-level appellate division, where Giuffra argued earlier this month that the case was âinfected by multiple fatal errors.â

Among those purported errors was the reliance on testimony from Michael Cohen, Trumpâs former personal lawyer and so-called âfixer,â who told the jury that he was ordered to pay Daniels $130,000 to keep quiet about a 2006 tryst she had with Trump. According to Cohen, he orchestrated similar payments for other women on Trumpâs behalf in the past.

But when it came time for Cohen to be repaid, he said Trump fudged business records to make it look like he was merely paying Cohen for standard legal fees.

Further trial testimony revealed Trump signed several of those scrutinized checks from the Oval Office during his first presidential term.

#7492. New Mexico city accused of violating free speech with panhandling ordinance

A woman arrested two years ago for panhandling in a northwestern New Mexico city wants a federal court to find a panhandling ordinance unconstitutional.

ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. â Rebecca Serrano-Himmel says she was sitting in a strip mall parking lot with a sign requesting money in March 2024 when police cited and trespassed her from the property. Four months later, she was arrested when displaying a similar sign at an intersection.

Two years after her arrest, she’s suing the northwestern New Mexico city of Farmington over its sweeping panhandling ban, arguing that holding a cardboard sign requesting money is constitutionally protected speech.

In her suit filed Monday in New Mexico federal court, Serrano-Himmel seeks damages against the city and its police officers for unreasonable seizure and deprivation of free speech, as well as a declaration that the ordinance violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution.

Farmington Mayor Nate Duckett, a defendant in the suit, signed the panhandling ordinance in February 2023. It prohibits the solicitation of money or goods on public and private property.

“Since the passing of the ordinance and still after the receipt of the letter alerting the mayor and the city attorney about the unconstitutionality of the ordinance, Duckett continued to enforce the panhandling ordinance in a manner that deprived multiple people of their first amendment right to free speech,” Serrano-Himmel writes in the complaint.

According to Serrano-Himmel, holding a sign requesting money in a public space is protected speech under the U.S. Constitution and the state constitution.

This ordinance allowed city police officers to cease her speech and retaliate against her as a result of her exercising her free speech, she says.

In her first run-in with city police in March 2024, Serrano-Himmel says Officer Aaron Favaloro seized her identification to check for outstanding warrants and issued a citation for panhandling and a trespass notice, despite having no ownership or control over the property.

Serrano-Himmel asserted throughout the interaction that she was engaging in lawful behavior. In response, Favaloro threatened to arrest her. She was found not guilty of panhandling in July 2024.

Two weeks later, city police officer Marcus Martinez approached Serrano-Himmel after spotting her walking in a parking lot with a sign stating she was homeless and requesting assistance.

Serrano-Himmel says Martinez told her she was panhandling, which was not allowed in city limits. She continued to state that she was acting lawfully. Martinez then arrested her for panhandling and criminal trespass and seized her sign.

The officers’ actions violate Serrano-Himmel’s First Amendment right, which protects her speech, and Fourth Amendment right, which protects her against unreasonable seizures, Serrano-Himmel writes in the complaint. Both officers are named as defendants in the suit, alongside Duckett and the city of Farmington.

Serrano-Himmel’s attorney, Joseph P. Kennedy of The Kennedy Law Firm, has challenged the ordinance before, according to Serrano-Himmel.

Kennedy gave notice to Farmington that non-party Jerry Sullivan was suing the city in August 2023 after Sullivan had been detained for panhandling.

Sherald Daniels, also represented by Kennedy, sued over the ordinance in another federal lawsuit earlier this year after receiving a citation for playing music in a public space.

“The city has enforced the ordinance repeatedly in a manner that has damaged and deprived the free-speech rights of residents and visitors,” Serrano-Himmel writes.

Farmington city attorneys declined to provide comment. Kennedy did not respond to a request for comment before publication.

RICHMOND, Va. (CN) â A Virginia school district that closed all 29 of its schools last week is now under an investigation to determine whether it mishandled sexual assault reports and violated Title IX, the Department of Education announced Monday.

Albemarle County Public Schools decided to temporarily close all of its schools after reporting 500 district employees had not undergone state-required background checks. While employees did complete fingerprint-based criminal background checks, they weren’t subject to a Virginia Department of Social Services search, which checks for child abuse complaints.

One district employee was arrested earlier this year on charges of sexual misconduct involving students, while another was booked for possession of child pornography.

On Monday, the U.S. Department of Education said it has directed Virginia to withhold federal funds from Albemarle County Public Schools and launched a civil rights investigation into the district., which plans to keep its schools closed for at least a week to give the Department of Social Services time to finish background checks.

Chandra Hayes, the district’s acting superintendent, said the department had cleared 519 of the 524 employees as of Monday, adding that the five remaining applications were returned due to clerical errors on the forms, which will be corrected and resubmitted. She said no employees will work with students until the Virginia Department of Social Services clears them.

âNothing matters more than the safety of our students. We share the U.S. Department of Educationâs goal of making sure every adult who works with children in our schools has been properly screened,â Hayes said. âThese issues are real, and fixing them takes time, commitment and accountability. Our students and families deserve a division that meets every obligation it has to them.â

Hayes pointed out that federal funds mainly support services for students with disabilities and those who are from low-income households.

In addition to the measures itâs taking against the school district, the Department of Education is placing the Virginia Department of Education on high-risk status for what the federal agency describes as an apparent failure to enforce state and federal laws.

âA school division needing to shutter the doors of its schools to ensure that students are not forced to interact with sexual predators is an unfathomable failure of the school division and its leaders,â U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said Monday. âParents should never have to question whether their childâs school is aiding or abetting child predators.â

In response to the department’s announcement, a Virginia Department of Education spokesman said Monday that her agency has taken a few measures to address the issues at the district.

âThe safety and well-being of all of Virginiaâs 1.2 million students is of the greatest importance, and the agency will continue to do everything in its power to protect students and ensure school divisions are in full compliance with the law,â said Alyssa Schwenk, the Assistant Superintendent of Strategic Communications at the Virginia Department of Education.

On Friday, Virginia state Senator R. Creigh Deeds and Delegate Katrina E. Callsen, both Democrats, announced Friday their plans to introduce legislation to address the issue, and a spokesperson for Democratic Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger’s office said her administration would continue its audit of the processes that led to the failures in the district.

“The Spanberger administration has zero tolerance for people in positions of public trust failing to protect children and will continue to engage aggressively to hold those individuals accountable,” said Libby Wiet, the governor’s communications director. “The governor is taking aggressive action to improve a system that has failed children, families and the community in Albemarle.”

Several Albemarle County School Board members did not respond to requests for comment Monday.

#7488. The Supreme Court and profanity

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

Around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. New York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

The station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”

Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he said was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”

The previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

Early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

Two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

At oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

One striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

Justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

The court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”

Stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

Justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”

Brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and said he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”

Brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:

Brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

Finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”

Brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

In closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

At the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC announced that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

In 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

The case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

In 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws shows the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”

Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

Recommended Citation: Anastasia Boden, The Supreme Court and profanity, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 23, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-supreme-court-and-profanity/

MIDDLETOWN, Iowa (AP) â The U.S. Army plans to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa on Wednesday morning after getting approval from a federal appeals court in a saga that has sowed confusion and included an unusual twist from President Donald Trump.

In an unusual twist, Trump, commander in chief of the Army, said on social media earlier in the day that in addition to the court’s go-ahead, he wanted Gov.-elect Rob Sand to approve the detonation. Sand, a Democrat who doesn’t take office until January, has said the decision is fully up to the Trump administration.

The detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide was initially planned for last Friday, but the Army has since changed the date three times following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. It said the weather was most favorable this coming Wednesday.

Environmentalists sued last week to stop the detonation at the site near Middletown, not far from the Mississippi River about 90 miles (140 km) south of Cedar Rapids. The court temporarily halted the permit, prompting the Army to argue that it didnât need authorization after all, given that it was an emergency.

An attorney for the environmentalists emphasized that their legal challenge centers on the validity of the EPA permit, not the Armyâs decision to move forward with the detonation under the emergency provision.

Earthjustice managing attorney Rachel Rintelmann said the lawsuit has alerted the public to the threat.

âToday, the 8th circuit decided to let the Army proceed with its plan, and we respect that decision," Rintelmann said in a statement Monday. “But the Army created this emergency through neglect, and it owes the people of Iowa more information about the planned detonation and more safeguards for their health.â

Sand said in a social media post on Monday that the administration should âmake this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks.â

On Sunday, Sand posted that because of previous decisions that have already been made, âNo good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been.â

Current Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the state emergency management office on Friday. The state also created a dedicated website for information about the operation.

A flight with Army officials bound for Iowa departed Joint Base Andrews to help support the Armyâs planned detonation before Trumpâs Truth Social post went out on Monday, two people familiar with the travel arrangements confirmed to the AP. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss travel details that had not been made public.

Flight tracking websites showed an Army business jet take off from the base just before 1 p.m. Trump posted minutes later.

Some residents near Middletown have been sealing their windows and doors as a precaution to keep out any lead dust that might result from the detonation. Others who live farther away were raising concern on social media about the possible paths that the plume could take depending on the wind.

Officials acknowledge that lead is toxic and have recommended that people stay indoors whenever the detonation happens and clean off outdoor surfaces with water afterward to limit exposure to any lead particles.

Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson said the detonation must take place âso we can move on with our lives.â

âImproper storage and disposal is where things go wrong,â he said on social media.

Leaders of states that border Iowa also expressed concern. Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are working to establish additional monitoring of air and water quality, public health and agriculture resources.

âBut I want to emphasize: this is a federal operation,â Kehoe said. âThe states of Iowa, Missouri and Illinois do not have a say on when this is conducted."

In court filings over the weekend, Army Col. Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency response specialist, explained that less liquid inside the barrels means the solution inside is more susceptible to freezing, which increases the sensitivity of the crystals that have formed around the inside of the rim and underside of the lids.

âEven a small amount of friction can break the crystal formation, causing an explosive chain reaction,â he said in his declaration to the court.

In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.

According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drumsâ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.

The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their court filings that other alternatives were not fully considered.

Officials contend that the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop in the coming days.

Lead azide is âvery sensitiveâ and also susceptible to heat, freezing, shock, friction and âall sorts of things that could cause an accidental detonation,â said John Goodpaster, a chemistry professor at Indiana University, Indianapolis. Itâs also old, which increases the risk because explosives become increasingly unstable as they age, he said.

Add in the environmental threat caused by the lead that will escape into the atmosphere and the challenge is significant, Goodpaster said.

âI do not envy the Army,â Goodpaster said. âThey are in a situation where theyâve got a large amount of very dangerous material and not very many good options in terms of trying to dispose of it.â

But itâs impossible to predict when it could explode on its own, he said.

âThe longer we wait, the longer the risk accumulates that they might have an accidental explosion,â Goodpaster said.

By SUSAN MONTOYA BRYAN and LAURA BARGFELD

#7486. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”

Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7482. The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”

According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

The Times story has reverberated quickly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and important source.

Both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

As most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “said in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:

The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

In fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

Scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

Returning to Heller and the phrase at issue, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

Rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”

Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

So how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam said that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

(Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”)

From there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at issue is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.)

This test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

This is particularly relevant since the court is currently preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more important problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.

Places’ mission is to help discerning global travelers find their favorite places wherever they go through expert curation and community trust.

As a Data Scientist on the Places by Raya team you will play a key role that will shape how the Places app uses data to drive business decisions. This hands-on role combines data modeling and reporting with product analysis and experimentation. While the product itself has existed since 2023 the culture is very much like a new start-up with leadership being heavily invested in this product space and this role being the first dedicated Data Scientist to this space and supported by a dedicated Data Engineer.

This will be a fun role for someone who wants to build data solutions from the ground up and help shape how the entire team uses insights. This person should be able to articulate best practices, develop new analytical frameworks that tie user actions to outcomes, and strike the right balance between analytical rigor and pragmatic business action.

Successful candidates will demonstrate technical skills, product expertise, and business acumen, and be enthusiastic about making a positive impact through timely execution. You are passionate about leveraging the power of data to drive product changes with quality and agility and can demonstrate sound judgment under uncertainty.

#7480. Another Disney creator deal: YouTube illusionist Zach King joins the Mouse House

Disney continues to prove that Netflix isn’t the only competitor sniffing around YouTube‘s top talent.

For their deal, 36-year-old L.A.-based King will make 10 original short-form videos, which Disney will have exclusive rights to distribute. Disney says the agreement “will also bring [King’s] signature illusions to new content for Disney+ and [King’s] own channels inspired by Disney’s Hexed, Star Wars, and other Disney films and experiences.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

One of the King projects coming to Disney+ is Cardboard Wars, his 52-minute intentionally-low-budget tribute to Star Wars: A New Hope. King uploaded the film to YouTube in August, and soon will cross-post it to Disney’s streaming service.

But there’s still more: King will pop up on Disney’s social accounts as well, hosting behind-the-scenes content about the VFX and filmmaking techniques he uses in his content.

“I fell in love with filmmaking and storytelling as a young kid, grabbing my parents’ home video camera and teaching myself to edit,” King wrote in an Instagram post. “A lot of my early homemade films were inspired by the Disney movies and the behind-the-scenes footage they would show in the DVD featurettes. There was always a sense of magic I would see on the screen, and so I’m thrilled to be working with Disney to continue that magic of filmmaking for the next generation of storytellers.”

King has worked with Disney regularly in recent months: He was at its glitzy Created in L.A. event in September, and earlier this month played a game of viral format Cake or Fake? with Hexed (and Arcane, and Sinners, and Spider-Verse, and Hawkeye) star Hailee Steinfeld. But this is his first official, expansive content deal.

“Zach makes the impossible look real, bringing the kind of imagination and originality that has always defined Disney,” Asad Ayaz, The Walt Disney Company’s CMO and Brand Officer, said in a statement. “He brings both a filmmaker’s ingenuity and a fan’s passion to our stories, along with a unique connection with audiences. We want to build lasting relationships with creators like Zach, giving their ideas room to grow across Disney. That’s what makes this next chapter of our work together so full of possibility.”

As we mentioned above, everyone–including YouTube–has had their eye on Netflix’s obvious poaching efforts…leaving room for Disney to sneak in the back.

In the last couple months, Disney has announced deals with major creators Dhar Mann, Dude Perfect, and Like Nastya. Crucially, these are all development deals–the exact kind of agreement that has YouTube on guard with Netflix.

And Disney’s not quite showing its full hand just yet. During its earnings call Nov. 17, executives only mentioned YouTubers once, in passing and in reference to Disney+’s growing crop of approved creator content.

We suspect more is in the pipeline–and that YouTube may have to start paying creators to turn down Disney deals, too.

This role makes sure the services they use are reliable, correctly authorized and observable. It is a systems and infrastructure role rather than a product AI role, and it is not an SRE role. You will build and operate these systems, not only advise on them.

This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments, owns what they ship in production, and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

Build and operate the production backend services behind Supabase’s AI products, including the MCP server: deployment, scaling, configuration and release.

Take ownership of how those services are structured, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

Define, measure and meet reliability targets for the services the team runs. Set SLOs with the SRE team, track error budgets, and use them to decide what to fix first.

Participate in the AI Tooling team on-call rotation, and be a first responder for incidents in those services. Investigate, fix, coordinate with other teams during incidents, and write the follow-ups and runbooks.

Work the AI Tooling team support queue alongside on-call, and turn recurring issues into fixes rather than repeated manual answers.

Own authentication and authorization for AI and agent clients: OAuth apps, scoped tokens, and permissions that make sense for agents as well as humans, including how we change or deprecate a permission without breaking existing integrations.

Own observability for the services the team runs: metrics, traces, logs, dashboards and alerts, so we find problems before customers do.

Handle capacity and abuse for agent traffic: rate limits, cost and safety controls, and behavior under load or when a dependency degrades.

Improve the architecture of the services the team owns as they grow, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

Work with the Platform team on shared code, review ownership and release process, and with the SRE team on infrastructure, alerting and incident practice.

Contribute to the code of the AI Tooling team’s tools, such as the MCP server, where it affects reliability and security, in partnership with the engineers who own the product surface.

Have 5+ years of experience building and running backend services in production, and have carried on-call for them.

Write strong TypeScript or Go, and are comfortable working in the other.

Have designed and operated APIs with real consumers: versioning, error handling, rate limiting, and backwards-compatible change.

Know OAuth, OIDC, JWT and API authorization well enough to debug them in production and to explain where implementations commonly deviate from the spec.

Have a good understanding of PostgreSQL and relational databases.

Are comfortable with CI/CD, Docker and containerized deployments, and with infrastructure as code. Any tool is fine.

Can debug across services: follow a slow or failing request through several systems using metrics, traces and logs.

Communicate clearly in writing, work with a wide range of stakeholders, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

Experience with agent tooling (MCP or similar), or serving traffic from AI agents and LLM clients.

Experience moving a service out of a larger codebase while keeping existing clients working.

Experience with Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Logflare or a similar observability stack, and real SLO work.

Open-source contributions, especially to Node.js, Go, TypeScript or API tooling.

#7477. Netflix is rallying post-Warner Bros. with revised IRL installation plans and a potential bid for NBCUniversal

OK, so Netflix failed to buy Warner Bros. Discovery.

That potential acquisition is apparently top of wishlist for Netflix (and Variety already deemed it “Hollywood’s Next Big Deal”), but Comcast co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts say they’re not selling.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Well, according to Bloomberg, the current plan is for Netflix to revamp its approach to permanent interactive IRL installations, aka Netflix Houses. The streamer first unveiled these in 2023, with a demo setup that looked like someone stocked the gift shop in Jurassic Park with merch of the laser murder doll from Squid Game.

At the time, Josh Simon, Netflix’s then-VP of Consumer Products (now CEO of collectibles company Funko) said the concept for Netflix Houses came from knowing “fans love to immerse themselves in the world of our movies and TV shows,” and “thinking a lot about how we take that to the next level.”

Netflix had flirted with pop-ups before that; those were mainly focused on selling stuff. Make no mistake, Netflix Houses are also focused on selling stuff, but in a Disney World kind of way, where fans pay $39 to enter the House and head through an art gallery-esque space filled with themed exhibits like exclusive theater shows, movie/TV set recreations, VR experiences, and arcade games. There are cafeterias and merch shops, but by and large the things to buy share billing with things to do.

The Houses are permanent installations (for now just in Dallas and Philly, with one planned to open in Vegas in 2027) but the exhibits within rotate regularly to keep up with whatever’s trending on Netflix.

This year, for example, the Houses were renovated to feature animated smash megahit KPop Demon Hunters. They’ve also spotlighted Stranger Things, One Piece, Wednesday, and the aforementioned Squid Game.

Per Bloomberg, Netflix initially planned to open dozens of Houses across the U.S., focusing on quieter suburban areas away from downtowns. It wanted to snap up spaces in malls, which are not doing very well and might be willing to rent for cheap.

But apparently the results from its first two Houses haven’t been quite what Neflix expected, so it’s pausing openings beyond Vegas until it can reassess.

People familiar with the matter told Bloomberg the Philadelphia location has daytime draws like mini golf and a movie theater, but doesn’t see much traffic at night. Dallas, meanwhile, is breaking even financially, and has done well with larger groups and corporate events.

Netflix is also planning to see what comes from its Las Vegas location. Vegas, as you may know, is not in fact a quieter suburban locale–so if the House there proves to be profitable, with more traffic than Dallas and Philly, Netflix could reconsider where it opens in the future.

People familiar with the matter said Netflix is also looking at maybe taking Houses overseas. But wherever the next one ends up, it probably won’t open for at least another year, they said, until significant data from all three flagship U.S. locations is in.

Now, with all this in mind, it’s worth remembering Netflix just shock-fired its longtime Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and replaced her with Peter Rice, Disney‘s former General Entertainment Chairman. Film chief Dan Lin is out too. Clearly, Netflix hopes to revamp more than its IRL installations…and perhaps it’s hoping Rice’s Disney EXP comes in handy with the Houses?

#7469. TikTok’s CSAM Problem; You Can’t Bank On Data Security

Different advertisers have different brand safety thresholds, but there are some topics that no one wants to be associated with. First and foremost: child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

That risk is now playing out in Spain, where several advertisers paused their TikTok ads this week.

Last week, Spanish news outlets reported that multiple advertisers – including Banco Santander and energy company Moeve – had suspended their TikTok campaigns after ads from major Spanish brands had appeared alongside CSAM on the platform.

Videos that either included CSAM or featured websites that sell CSAM ran before or after ads from 21 brands, Digiday reports, including Banco Santander, Samsung, Ralph Lauren and Pringles.

TikTok has avoided taking direct responsibility in its recent statements, assuring advertisers and agencies in a note that it is “deeply committed” to ensuring that TikTok is a safe platform for teens and that it has a task force addressing the issue.

“We condemn child sexual abuse and exploitation,” a spokesperson tells Digiday (uh, duh), adding that it’s “categorically prohibited” on the platform.

But, so far, these statements have done little to convince advertisers to return.

“Until we know what’s happening, it’s better to pause,” Laura Camazón, head of digital and innovation at Mediaplus Equmedia tells Digiday. So far, three of the agency’s clients have paused their TikTok activity.

In a week of mass technology service outages across America, Chase wants you to know that its regular service has not been disrupted.

However, one or more of Chase’s third-party tech vendors was the victim of a cyberattack. “We believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” the bank wrote in a statement on Thursday.

Mastercard and Visa were also tagged by a ransomware hacker org that leaked customer data. Credit card numbers were not compromised, but the data included some customer details. A Mastercard spokesperson described the leak as only touching a “limited amount of information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” The Wall Street Journal reports.

The disclosures leave many key questions unanswered. None of the companies has named the vendors involved or specified whose data was exposed and what it included. For example, did the leaked data belong to cardholders who consented to having their data used for marketing and analytics? That would be an interesting wrinkle.

Chase was a little more specific about next steps, though, at least.

“Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” it said in its response.

On Thursday, Anthropic IPO’d at a cool $2 trillion, making it the first of the leading AI companies to go public.

Its share price opened at $111.50, then dropped to roughly $100 within its first hour on the market.

The timing is striking. Anthropic’s public launch comes just a week after ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down from his role at the company, following a leaked affair with a woman rumored to be a Chinese spy.

Huang’s departure left a gaping hole in AI funding. The industry may miss him for other reasons, too, but the bigger concern is capital.

“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Shamillah Bankiya, a partner at Dawn Capital, tells TechCrunch. Colette Kress, Huang’s temporary replacement as Nvidia’s CEO, is expected to be “much more conservative,” another investor adds.

Still, Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO goes to show that the AI bubble isn’t at risk of popping quite yet.

But it certainly “contrasts with an anxious moment for investors,” The New York Times writes, amid growing concerns over AI regulation and public backlash against the technology.
